Select groups of predictors

Source: vignettes/articles/predictor-groups.Rmd
predictor-groups.Rmd

A categorical predictor can require several contrasts, and a smooth effect can require several spline coefficients. The group argument selects such terms together. It also supports groups of related measurements. Adaptive ridge uses the squared Euclidean norm of the coefficients within each group, so positive and negative effects contribute equally to selection.

Fit and tune grouped predictors 

library(L0glm)
set.seed(41)
X <- matrix(rnorm(200*12),200,12)
group <- rep(1:6,each=2)
group[11:12] <- 0
beta <- c(1.5,-1.5,0,0,1,-1,rep(0,6))
y <- 1+as.numeric(X%*%beta)+rnorm(200)
fit <- l0glmFit(X,y,group=group,intercept=TRUE,lambda='gic',relaxed=TRUE)
l0glmMetrics(fit)[c('gic','group_support_size','group_df')]
#>        gic group_support_size group_df
#> 1 556.4179                  2        4

Group labels can be integers, characters or factors in any order. Group 0, the intercept and always.include terms are unpenalized. Explicit starting-zero exclusions remain binding; the returned sparse coefficient matrix retains all original predictor rows. A relaxed refit removes shrinkage on the retained groups.

For multiple outcomes, grouped=FALSE selects each predictor group independently within each channel. grouped=TRUE pools its coefficients across channels. Joint multinomial fits pool the identifiable CLR coefficients across categories.

cv <- l0glmTune(X,y,family=gaussian(),group=group,intercept=TRUE,relaxed=TRUE,
  tune='cv',nfolds=5,nlambda=10)
predict(cv$fit_1se,X[1:5,])

Every CV training fold repeats selection independently. Automatic local refinement tests whole-group additions, removals and exchanges when the initial selected coefficient dimension is at most 50. See predictor groups for the penalty equations and local refinement for its controls. Predictor-group models currently fit the supplied design directly; use screen='none' when its dimensions would otherwise activate automatic ISIS.

GIC and group size

The reported information criteria use the same parameter-count convention as other L0glm models:

\mathrm{GIC}=-2\ell(\widehat B,\widehat\psi) +\log(p)\log\log(n)\,k.

Here k counts free nonzero coefficients, compulsory coefficient dimensions and estimated noise parameters. Multinomial counts respect the CLR zero-sum constraint. The original selectable predictor count p is retained. A selected group of four unrestricted coefficients contributes four parameters; its size is accounted for through those coefficients. No further group-size multiplier enters the reported GIC. See information criteria for the Fan–Tang GIC and its assumptions.

To calibrate adaptive-ridge block selection, named IC presets use nominal group coefficient dimensions as penalty multipliers. Exact boundary zeros can reduce the reported parameter count of the resulting fit. IC tuning and local refinement evaluate that returned support using the parameter-count criterion above. A numeric lambda instead specifies a penalty per selected group, with optional group.multiplier values; group_objective reports this weighted group target. Stored multipliers permit numerical reproduction of an IC-calibrated ridge fit.

Other group-specific selection criteria are possible. For example, Zhang et al. study a group-count criterion in Gaussian best-subset-of-groups regression. L0glm retains its parameter-count GIC across families and uses it consistently in the comparisons below.

Comparisons with grpreg

These four simulations include equal and unequal group sizes, correlated predictors and signed effects. Each is repeated with three independent seeds. Two compulsory predictors and an intercept are retained in every method. The reproduction script compares L0glm with grpreg’s group LASSO, group MCP and group SCAD, using both information-criterion paths and five-fold CV with shared folds.

The GIC comparisons use one common likelihood and count active coefficients. For Gaussian data the variance is known to be one, which makes the score comparable even for nearly interpolating path fits. L0glm’s estimated-scale fits are included as a diagnostic alongside the known-scale fits. The grpreg paths contain 40 lambda values; L0glm uses its GIC preset or a ten-value CV grid. This common scoring choice is distinct from grpreg’s default shrinkage-based effective degrees of freedom, described in its selection documentation.

Gaussian preset fits recover the groups accurately, with prediction errors close to the noise level in the equal-size case. The grpreg Gaussian path solvers are particularly fast. In logistic regression, L0glm’s preset with local refinement is faster than these complete paths; the unequal-size, correlated example is harder for parameter-count GIC, and CV recovers more of its true groups.

Timings are medians; recovery scores are averages across three replicates. All fits and CV folds use one thread, on an HP ZBook Fury G8 with an Intel Core i9-11950H, Windows, R 4.5.0 and grpreg 3.6.0. Simulation and final scoring are excluded from the timings. The complete run-level results include test RMSE or AUC/log loss, convergence diagnostics and path warnings.
